title: Wings as eagles (Isaiah 40:31)
hookLine: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength"

lines: MY WAY IS HIDDEN FROM THE LORD.
cards: Near the end of Isaiah forty, the prophet quotes the people's complaint back to them. Jacob is saying: my way is hidden from the Lord, my cause is passed over. Nobody sees what this is costing me.
The prophet answers with a question, hast thou not known?, and says the Lord fainteth not.
Then he grants that the tiredness is real for people: even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. So where does strength come from, if not from being young?
The chapter's last verse answers, with wings in it.

teach.h: THEY THAT WAIT, OR THEY THAT HOPE.
teach.b: The verse reads: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Start with the condition.
Not they that try harder. Not they that are young. They that wait.
Here strength isn't something you grind out; it's given back while you wait. Some translations render that verb as they that hope.

teach.h: FLY, RUN, WALK: THE ORDER GOES DOWN.
teach.b: Now the order of the promise: fly, run, walk. A pep talk would build up: walk, then run, then soar. Isaiah goes the other way.
Some readers hear that as honest.

teach.h: WALK, AND NOT FAINT, IS STRENGTH TOO.
teach.b: There are days of wings and days you can run, and plenty of days when the most anyone can promise is that you'll walk and not faint. The verse counts that as strength too, and lists it last, where it has the final word.

teach.h: AN EAGLE RISES ON MOVING AIR.
teach.b: And the eagle: the Hebrew word is nesher, a great bird of the open sky. Some readers picture it rising on what's already moving in the air, not flapping its way up.
Waiting, in this verse, looks less like doing nothing and more like being still enough to be carried. Jewish life builds that stillness into the week.
Shabbat is one way a whole people practices stopping, so the strength can come back.

how: Jews read Isaiah 40 as part of the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and Shabbat is the weekly practice of stopping work so that body and spirit can rest.

o: wings, a picture of God's sheltering care
eagle, a great bird of the open sky
dove, the bird sent out from the ark

games.q: wings as eagles — tap the pairs.

s: in the verse, strength comes from being young
even the youths faint. strength is renewed in those who wait.
the promise ends with walking, not flying
fly, run, walk: the order goes down, and walking and not fainting still counts.
the people in the chapter feel seen by God
they complain that their way is hidden from the Lord.

games.q: you're worn out, and even the young and strong around you are falling. what does the verse say renews strength?
games.why: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength." waiting, not effort, is the condition.

practice: Breathe out longer than you breathe in, and let your shoulders drop. Don't fix, plan or check anything; let today be whatever kind of day it is, a wings day, a running day or a walking day, since all three count.
If you pray, you can hold the verse's first words: they that wait upon the Lord.

wordCard.voice: Nesher. Hebrew for eagle, the bird in Isaiah forty, thirty-one: those who wait shall renew their strength, mount up, run, and walk and not faint. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: renew your strength. Walking, and not fainting, is strength too. Rest well, and see you soon.

sources.q: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
